_comment: EXAMPLE — stage 3 output, merged. One file per use case, named <use case id>.json, holding every threat from all six letters. THIS IS WHAT STAGE 4 READS. The per-letter files in ./<use case id>/ are stage 3's working artifacts and its cache unit; stage 4 can ignore them. Files starting with '_' are examples and are never analyzed.
name: Registered customer signs in with email and password

threats.title: Credential stuffing against an unthrottled login endpoint
threats.description: The login route compares credentials with no rate limit, lockout, or CAPTCHA, so an attacker may guess passwords without bound.
threats.attack_scenario: The attacker replays a breach corpus of email/password pairs against POST /rest/user/login. With no throttling, a few thousand requests surface accounts whose owners reused a password.

evidence.snippet: const user = await models.User.findOne({ where: { email, password: hash(password) } })

threats.recommendation: Rate limit the login route by both source address and target account, and add escalating delay after repeated failures.

threats.title: Passwords stored with a fast unsalted hash
threats.description: Credentials are hashed with MD5, which is fast and unsalted, so a single database read compromises every account.
threats.attack_scenario: An attacker who obtains the user table through any read primitive recovers common passwords with a commodity GPU in seconds, then reuses them here and on other services.
threats.recommendation: Replace with bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2id at a tuned work factor, and rehash on next successful login.

threats.title: Authentication outcomes are never logged
threats.description: Neither successful nor failed logins produce an audit record, so an account takeover cannot be distinguished after the fact from legitimate use.
threats.attack_scenario: An attacker authenticates with stolen credentials and changes the account email. With no log of either action the operator cannot establish when access began, or whether the owner did it themselves.
threats.recommendation: Emit a structured record for both outcomes carrying user id, source address, UTC timestamp, and a request correlator, to an append-only sink.

_notes.shape: Every threat from all six letters, concatenated. Three shown here; a real use case typically yields fifteen to thirty.
_notes.sorting: risk is derived from likelihood x impact through a fixed matrix identical in all six skills, so ordering by it is meaningful: critical, high, medium, low.
_notes.filtering: confidence 'high' guarantees at least one evidence entry with a real file and line — filter to it for the citable subset of the report.
_notes.coverage: import coverage_table from main.contract for threats-per-letter counts, and validate_merged to catch duplicate ids or a letter that returned nothing.
